content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This is paper proposes a new approach to the  depth  completion problem, where an image is provided  together with a sparse  depth map  that  must be filled.
It proposes to join together a convolutional attention layer and a transformer layer to improve the  performance of a U-Net end-to-end backbone for the problem. The goal is to  simultaneously model local as well as global relationships in the image and depth map.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The proposed CompletionFormer architecture (Fig.2) is followed  by a "SPN  refinement" (actually, NLSPN) that improves the final depth. The authors justify the refinement by mentioning  that "Depth by direct regression from U-Net is still blurry and misaligned". This seems to  suggest that the proposed  approach does not work on its own.
This is verified in the ablation study  (Table 2) where the  method by itself (J) performs much  worse than the method with refinement (G & K), with a MAE performance drop of 17.0mm and 17.1mm, respectively.

Observing that the MAE performance drop  between results (M & N) versus (H) is 0.3mm and 0.4mm, respectively, the authors mention "It confirms that local and global contexts are vital for depth completion", which is not obvious at all since the improvement  is so small.

Given these ablation results, the correct conclusion, as the author  mention itself ("Refinement is also crucial for depth completion methods") is  that the NLSPN refinement is not only vital for depth completion,  but also that the proposed method  does not significantly improve performance of  the  NLSPN refinement run without it.

In Table 2b, the "scanline" sparsity results are hard  to  understand. The  role of 1,4,16,64 scanlines  is unclear. The 64 scanlines results suggest that all  methods essentially perform the same.

Results featuring depth maps (Figure 4 and 5) are hard to interpret because of  low resolution  and hard to distinguish colors.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Overall,  the  paper is well written and clear.  Only the qualitative (Fig.4 & 5) should  be improved as they are hard to read.

The proposed  approach  is  novel, but fails, in  our opinion, to convince  that it provides any significant  increase in performance, as it crucially depends on another method (NLSPN) to provide competitive results.
content.summary_of_the_review: An interesting approach to depth completion was proposed, but it fails to  demonstrate its usefulness.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper describes a depth completion model that takes in sparse depth observations and an RGB image and outputs a dense depth map. It combines several existing techniques (most notably, pyramid vision transformer, CBAM, NLSPN) and shows state-of-the-art performance on the outdoor KITTI Depth Completion benchmark and the indoor NYUv2 dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 

* On some metrics, the method ranks top on the two considered benchmarks. 

* The key components (pyramid vision transformer, CBAM, NLSPN) are well-known powerful tools, and their uses in the model appear to be well-motivated and fitting. 

Weaknesses: 

* If we focus on RMSE, the proposed method is among the worse on KITTI (see Tab. 4). It's doing a bit better on NYUv2, but still not showing a clear advantage. 
* The key components are all from prior work, and the model can be seen as an improved version of NLSPN where the computation blocks are enhanced with ViT and CBAM. The contribution is particularly questionable given how similar the proposed method performs compared to NLSPN (Tab. 4). 
* The proposed model essentially provides a dense-to-dense mapping. The paper does not explain much about why the model is particularly suitable for depth completion. Exploring potential use cases for other dense prediction tasks can expand the impact of the work. 
* Some inconsistency: it says in Sec.4.6 that "our model trained with only L1 loss" while earlier, it's mentioned that "a combined L1 and L2 loss is employed". Is the same model used consistently throughout the experiments? 
* Some issues with clarity -- details in the next section.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The work is technically sound and comes with a sufficient amount of details and experiments. 

Clarity can be improved: 
* It's not clear what Fig.1 is trying to show -- none of the heat maps highlight the target object. 
* Some terms are not defined clearly enough and do not seem to match what's in Fig.2: "the fused result from the decoder is concatenated with features from stage one and fed to the first convolution layer of the prediction head. Its output is concatenated with the raw feature from RGB and depth embedding module" 
* Inaccurate depiction in Fig.2: SPN Refinement takes not only initial depth estimation.
content.summary_of_the_review: The work has quite limited contribution considering that (1) it can be seen as a slightly enhanced NLSPN and the additions are mostly from previous work and (2) there's no clear improvement over NLSPN.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a network design and training method for depth completion in this paper. The core contribution is the design of an integrated layer block that can utilize the complementary advantages of convolutional layers and transformers. The network architecture composed of these blocks shows experimental results that outperform existing depth completion competitors.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper is well-written, and the claimed contributions are clear. Several experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithm shows SOTA performance in the depth completion field. These experiments are sufficiently voluminous to prove that the algorithm outperformed its competitors with a smaller amount of computation. As another advantage, the authors reviewed the performance of the proposed algorithm at various network complexity settings, which is a good indication that the proposed algorithm can work effectively in various situations that may exist in practice.

The approach of this paper is combinatorial (a structure that integrates CNN, attention, and transformer) and lacks novelty. I think the authors should have duly covered more related work before proposing a new module (combining CNN and transformer) which is the most significant contribution of the paper. For example, the paper below has a similar motivation to this paper.
   - CMT: Convolutional neural networks meet vision transformers (CVPR 2022)
Addressing more similar studies and clarifying differences will improve the paper's quality.

Another contribution, 'Effect in situations where depths are captured more sparsely,' seems to need more validation. From the experiments on NYUv2 in Table 3, I am not sure if this algorithm will perform better in a more sparse environment. What about the performance of the proposed algorithm and its competitors for smaller sample numbers (extreme situations like 50, 10, or 1)?

The following is a question from the implementation side.
How are missing values of sparse depth in the input of the network handled? For example, is it entered as a specific value (such as 0m)? Or do you use some other alternative (e.g., additional input channels to tell you valid/invalid values)?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I think the clarity and quality of this paper are good. Algorithms are incremental rather than completely novel. The description in this paper is sufficiently reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: In my opinion, this study has some areas for improvement but it is acceptable.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors in this paper propose a method for performing depth completion on sparse observations made by noisy sensors by introducing a Unet-like architecture that combines transformers with convolutional (channel-wise and spatial) attention, with a motivation to capture both the global (transformer) as well as the local features. Besides, the authors suggest using a unified-encoder model for both the RGB and sparse depth observations and fusing the multi-modal information early in the network. 
Empirical evaluations on the NYUv2 and KITI depth completion datasets show that the encoder unification as well as the proposed transformer/conv-attention dual modeling help the model be competitive as compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
* The proposed method is simple yet competitive in the compared benchmarks. 
* The proposed model is computationally significantly more efficient than the transformer-based models.
* The paper is reasonably easy to follow.
* The method suggests improvement in a meaningful problem; an effective combo of ML and sensory measurements to recover issues with both approaches.

Weaknesses:
* Technical novelties in the proposed method are existing but are rather not strong.
* The margin of improvement from the major contribution (transformer/convolutional attention combo), is rather marginal. The more substantial improvements are seemingly coming from the encoder-unification, and most significantly from the iterative refinement taken from an existing work. 
* Despite savings in compute as compared to the pure transformer model, even the smallest model (ours-tiny: ~389GFLOPs) seems rather expensive for being used in real practice for many of the applications that require depth completion, e.g. in AR/VR usecases.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
Please further clarify the following points:
* Combining the ability to effectively capture global (transformer) and local (convolutional) inter-dependencies is the main motivation for the proposed design of the network modules. However, the convolutional module is actually captured by the attention mechanism that is still generally a global operation. Are the convolution operations before the attention? Please clarify.
 * The authors mention "features from U-Net backbone are shared for estimating affinity matrix w, non-local neighbors, confidence map and initial depth D0 estimation" Please further clarify how exactly are the affinity matrix and the nonlocal neighbors created. Is the former a prediction with wxh (normalized) channels or created based on a similarity measure over a predicted feature map?
* Why are the non-local neighbors and affinity weights considered as two separate entities and as the same representation?
*  $w_\{u, v}(0, 0)$ notation used for the persistence of the initial prediction at $u, v$ is a confusing notation as with zero-indexing, 0, 0 could itself be a non-local neighbor coordinate; which would further simplify the limits of the equation after eq (2).
* The iterative refinement seems to be negligible in compute (e.g. only 0.6 GFLOPs in ours-small). Please clarify how significant this is in compute time given that the operations are sequential inherently. 
* That would help to add compute comparisons to table 4.
* It would be interesting to see the gains of the different number of refinement iterations $K$ and when it saturates.
* The "ours-base" model is only appearing in table 2(a) in the paper and it is worse than "ours-small" in all metrics. It seems that the authors can safely omit this model from the paper.


Reproducibility:
While certain details on the model architecture (Table 5 and Fig. 2), and some of the hyperparameters such as the learning rate schedule are specified, some more details, such as the scheme for affinity, non-local neighborhood, and the exact way to incorporate uncertainty in the updates are not specified. 
Besides, the authors haven't mentioned the source code release for the project. Of course, code release could have significantly helped the reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review:
In general, while the paper improves the SOTA models in depth completion in accuracy/efficiency optimal trade-off, the technical contributions are not significant. Besides, the accuracy gains by the major contribution (transformer/conv-attention combination) are limited.
Several further clarifications are needed to improve the clarity and reproducibility of the paper. 
Given the above, I rate the paper as 6, acknowledging the merits but also flagging room for improvements.

content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
